title: Where is wealth kept safe?
claim: Across the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth, a run of verses turns the hoarder's own logic of keeping against him. Feeding the destitute is the place to deposit wealth (226, வைப்புழி; Parimelazhagar: what is so given comes back to help the giver), while those who keep what they own lose it (228, வைத்திழக்கும்), eating alone to fill one's store is worse than begging (229), the man who does not even use his heap is as dead (1001), and wealth withheld from the destitute ages unused like a beauty growing old alone (1007). The positive side recurs in three chapters: shared food keeps hunger from the sharer (227), keeps his line from failing (44), and gain belongs only to those who, like the crow, call others before eating (527).
limits: The book does not rest giving on return alone: 228 names giving's own joy and 222 calls giving good even if there were no higher world. 82 and 229 condemn the solitary meal by comparison rather than by consequence, and the protective results in 44, 227 and 527 are asserted, not argued.

title: Giving and the manner that goes with it
claim: The book rarely praises giving bare: it pairs it with a glad face, sweet words, no scorn or no anger, and once ranks the manner above the gift, since 92 says a glad face and sweet speech are better than giving with a glad heart. 953 lists smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning flatly as marks of a good lineage (Parimelazhagar: the way one meets the poor who come), and 1057 shows why scorn matters, since the asker rejoices at giving without contempt, while 224 has the giver's own unease end only at the asker's glad face. In the Book of Wealth the same pair becomes an instrument: giving with sweet words wins the world for a king (387) and surrounds a man with kin (525), and 526 swaps sweet speech for not cherishing anger; Parimelazhagar on 525 matches the pair to the northern texts' dana and sama.
limits: 92 sits in the chapter praising sweet speech and may be that chapter's emphasis rather than a fixed ranking. Other verses define real giving by its recipient, not its manner (221, 223), and 387 and 525 treat giving as a means to loyalty, which is not the same claim as 92's ethical ranking.

title: One word for two shames
claim: 1011 splits நாண் in two: real shame is shame at one's deeds, and the rest is the shame of women of fair brow (Parimelazhagar: restraint of mind, speech and body proper to women of family). The Book of Love's shame is the second kind: in 1163 and 1247 it is, on Parimelazhagar's reading, what stops the woman telling him or going to him, and in 1251 it is the bolt on the door of restraint. Yet the Book of Love prizes that shame in the first kind's terms: it is the ornament that makes jewels needless (1089, as moral shame is the ornament of the worthy in 1014), and it is held dearer than life (Parimelazhagar on 1297; 1163's life strained on the pole), which is the valuation 1017 gives moral shame.
limits: The love verses are dramatised speeches, and the bridge to 1014 and 1017 is partly the commentator's: 1297 itself does not say shame is dearer than life. Kalaignar reads 1014 as remorse for a fault and Pope translates நாண் in 1017 as modesty, so the line between the two shames is drawn differently by different readers.

title: In the Book of Love shame never holds
claim: Several lover-speakers set shame against desire, and in none of them does shame survive; what varies is how it goes. 1247 puts the choice to the heart (give up desire or shame, I cannot bear both); 1132 makes it by decision, setting shame aside to ride the palmyra horse; in 1134 the flood of love carries shame off and in 1251 the axe of desire breaks the door it bolted; in 1297 it is forgotten in his absence, and in 1257 it is simply not felt in his presence (Parimelazhagar: on his return from another woman). Read together, the dilemma 1247 states is settled by force, forgetting or reunion as often as by choice.
limits: These are separate dramatised moments, and reading them as one sequence follows the chapter order, not any statement in the text. 1163 holds love and shame in balance without a loss, and 1149 is about shame at gossip rather than at desire. The man also loses shame by force in 1134, which qualifies the existing gender_asymmetry contrast between his choosing and her bearing.
